extracted.intended_audience: general readers and participants in 19th-century political/economic debate (citizens debating tariffs and reform)
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-19th-century public debate speech arguing for a protective tariff and making moral/historical remarks about reformers; combines political-economy propositions with rhetorical examples. Intended to persuade audiences about the policy necessity of protectionism and the moral standing of reformers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I: Domestic industry diversity for prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Nation which would be prosperous, must prosecute various branches of industry, and supply its vital Wants mainly by the Labor of its own Hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and illustration: historical pattern shows nations that depend principally on exporting agricultural staples and importing manufactures tend to be comparatively poor and ultimately dependent; merchant/commerce elites may flourish while producers famish (examples: Egypt behind Alexandria, southern Russia/Poland). This is proposed as a general law of national prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition II: New-country tendency toward staple-export/maunfacture-import
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural tendency in a comparatively new Country to become and continue an Exporter of Grain and other rude Staples and an Importer of Manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: new countries have abundant fertile soil and demand for labor to clear/build, while older countries have cheap labor, capital, and machinery; absent counteracting policy the new country will import manufactures and pay with agricultural staples. This is treated as empirically confirmed by universal experience (U.S. history 1782–90 cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition III: Harm of remaining dependent on foreign manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is injurious to the New Country thus to continue dependent for its supplies of clothing and Manufactured Fabrics on the Old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed economic reasoning: the price of exported staples is governed by the most distant/least favorable market (price there less transport costs determines local price). Example calculations (wheat prices, transport costs) show nominal savings on imported cloth are outweighed by depressed grain prices and heavy transport tolls; illustrative numeric example contrasts a quarter-million nominal saving vs nearly two million loss in aggregate value to the agricultural region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of price adjustment for exported staples
rubrics_metrics.description: The ruling price of Grain (as of any Manufacture) in a region whence it is considerably exported will be its price at the point to which it is exported, less the cost of such transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to show that distant markets (e.g., England) govern the local price of grain in exporting regions; thus sending surplus to poor distant markets drags down local prices. Examples: specific numeric transport and market price figures for wheat (e.g., costs from Illinois to New York and England).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign manufacturers can and will undercut to destroy nascent domestic industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign manufacturers, having cheaper labor, better machinery, and more abundant capital, can temporarily supply a foreign market at a small profit or even sacrifice to drive young domestic rivals out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: after 1815–16 British manufactures were sold in U.S. markets at 'one pound for pound' (large discounts) to break American factories; William Cobbett's admitted activities. Point: temporary sacrifice by established foreign producers will crush infant domestic manufacturing unless protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple 'buy where cheapest' (Free Trade) is misleading — hidden terms of trade costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Buying the cheapest foreign product may yield immediate cash savings but imposes larger hidden costs in depressed prices for domestic staples and increased dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical illustration: Illinois may save $250,000 buying cloth cheaper but lose nearly $2,000,000 in net proceeds on grain due to depressed prices when forced to sell surplus abroad — demonstrating that arithmetic of 'four simple rules' ignores the terms-of-trade/market-structure effects and transport tolls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agriculture is structurally disadvantaged in distant exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: Agriculture's products, by their perishability, bulk, and transport costs, are more exposed to disadvantage in distant exchange than manufactures; therefore agricultural regions suffer more when forced to exchange for imported manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative assertion: foreign manufactured goods can be sent to Illinois for perhaps 2–5% of their cost, while Illinois must pay 30–200% of value in transport to get staples to foreign consumers. This asymmetry justifies protecting domestic manufactures to avoid ruinous exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect industries most exposed to ruinous foreign rivalry
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the interest of the whole country that that portion of its Industry which is most exposed to ruinous foreign rivalry should be cherished and sustained by Protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that protection is not a sectional or narrow subsidy but a national policy: manufactures, commerce, and navigation all need protection; protecting manufactures also protects agricultural interests by creating local markets and improving terms of trade. Metaphor: one would not fortify only coastal cities and leave interior industry undefended.

rubrics_metrics.name: The worth of reforming ideas is independent of reformers' personal failings
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are often weak and fallible in action, even though their intellectual perception of the right is of the deepest and clearest; Bacon's philosophy is sound though Bacon was corrupt; Galileo's hypothesis is true though he recanted; Peter might have denied without belittling what he witnessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a standard for judging reformers: the truth of reforms (philanthropy, Christianity, moral ideas) is not negated by the moral failings of those who promulgate them. The passage gives multiple historical examples to illustrate separating person from idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of a reformer's greatness: the hostility he provokes
rubrics_metrics.description: The most striking tribute to the position and merits of the true Reformer is embodied in the universal jeer and shout which announces the exposure of the fallen aspirant or false pretender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: when vice and self-interest jeer at a reformer or exult at his fall, this often indicates that the reformer had been a real threat to entrenched interests; the stones hurled while living become the tombs of dead prophets — a measure of daring and truth of their utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: True reformers act from necessity and principle, not ease or ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: The true soldiers (reformers) never choose their course as the way of ease, of ambition, or from any selfish consideration whatever, but because it is the way of Right: 'Necessity is upon me,' says the true Apostle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with conservatives who view religion as a subordinate machinery of police; reformers insist on Humanity as the inevitable manifestation of all true religion and press that devoted, loving life answers imperfect faith. Examples include Daniel vs Nebuchadnezzar and the Baptist vs Herod.
